passages.p1:
For nearly a century, standardised examinations have served as the great equaliser of modern education. A single paper, set and marked by an impartial authority, promises that a student from a remote village and one from a metropolitan school are judged by the same yardstick. Defenders of the system argue that, whatever its flaws, it curbs favouritism and gives talent a chance to surface regardless of connections. Critics, however, contend that the yardstick itself is crooked. Because examinations reward the ability to recall and reproduce, they favour students who can afford coaching and rehearsal, while penalising those whose gifts lie in curiosity, judgement or collaboration. The result, they say, is not an equal contest but a well-disguised advantage for the already prepared.
A third group takes a more pragmatic view: abolishing examinations would only replace a visible inequality with hidden ones, such as interviews, in which personal contacts count for even more. They propose reforming rather than discarding the system, by setting questions that test reasoning, by allowing multiple attempts, and by publishing the weightage of each topic in advance. Whether such reforms can be introduced without making papers either too easy or too unpredictable remains the central difficulty, and it is one on which neither side has yet offered a convincing answer.
passages.p2:
Public libraries were once judged by a simple measure: how many books they lent. By that standard, many have been declining for years, as readers shift to screens and borrowing falls. Yet a growing number of librarians argue that the measure itself is outdated. A modern library, they say, is less a warehouse of books than a shared room in which people can study without paying, apply for jobs, learn to use unfamiliar software, or simply sit in the company of others. For a student without a quiet home, or a retiree living alone, such a space can matter more than any single title on the shelves.
Some councils have nevertheless treated libraries as an easy saving, reasoning that anything available online no longer needs a building. This reasoning overlooks the fact that access to the internet is itself unequal, and that the people who most need a free, staffed and reliable space are often the very ones without good connections at home. Closing a branch may therefore save money on paper but cost the community far more in lost opportunity. The case for libraries, in other words, rests not on nostalgia for paper, but on a plain calculation of who would be left behind without them.
passages.p3:
It is tempting to regard sleep as a pause in the working day, a period in which the mind simply switches off. Research over several decades has pointed to a very different picture. During sleep, the brain appears to replay the events of the waking hours, strengthening some memories and quietly discarding others. Experiments in which volunteers learn a task in the evening and are tested the next morning have repeatedly found that those who slept soundly perform better than those who stayed awake for the same period, even when the waking group was given time to rest. The benefit is not confined to simple facts; studies suggest that sleep may also help people notice patterns that had escaped them while awake, which is why a problem that seemed hopeless at midnight sometimes looks straightforward at dawn.
None of this, researchers caution, means that sleep can substitute for study. A student who has not learnt anything has nothing for the sleeping brain to consolidate. What the findings do suggest is that the common habit of sacrificing sleep to cram for an examination may be self-defeating, trading a few extra hours of exposure to the material for a weaker ability to retain it. The sensible approach, therefore, is to treat sleep as part of preparation rather than as a rival to it.
passages.p4: The first rains of the season (1) the town's market back to life. Vendors who had spent the dry months sitting idle now (2) their stalls with umbrellas, raincoats and plastic sheets, and the lane outside the old temple becomes a river of colourful canopies. Although the downpour often (3) traffic for hours, nobody seems to mind; shoppers simply wait under awnings, sipping hot tea and (4) the price of onions. By evening, when the clouds finally clear, the pavements are slick, the air smells of wet earth, and the sellers pack up with the quiet satisfaction of people who have (5) a good day's trade. Children, who were kept indoors for much of the afternoon, run out to splash through the puddles, and the lamps come on one by one along the lane.

questions.text: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (1) in the passage.
questions.explanation: 'The first rains' is plural and the passage is in the present tense, so the plain form 'bring' is needed.
questions.trap: Choosing 'brings' because 'season' is singular.
wrongReasons: Singular verb with the plural subject 'rains'
Past tense does not fit the present-tense passage
The participle leaves the clause without a main verb
steps: Spot what the question tests: Subject-verb agreement in cloze.
Option B (brings) is out: Singular verb with the plural subject 'rains'.
Option C (brought) is out: Past tense does not fit the present-tense passage.
Option D (bringing) is out: The participle leaves the clause without a main verb.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing 'brings' because 'season' is singular.
So the answer is option A: bring.

questions.text: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (2) in the passage.
questions.explanation: To 'stock' a stall is to fill it with goods for sale; the usual collocation is 'stock … with'.
questions.trap: Choosing 'store' because it sounds close in meaning.
wrongReasons: 'Stoke' means to feed a fire
'Store' would put the goods away, not display them on stalls
'Stack their stalls' is not an idiomatic phrase
steps: Spot what the question tests: Collocations: stock with.
Option A (stoke) is out: 'Stoke' means to feed a fire.
Option C (store) is out: 'Store' would put the goods away, not display them on stalls.
Option D (stack) is out: 'Stack their stalls' is not an idiomatic phrase.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing 'store' because it sounds close in meaning.
So the answer is option B: stock.

questions.text: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (3) in the passage.
questions.explanation: The downpour stops traffic for hours, so 'halts' fits. 'Hastens' contradicts the idea of waiting under awnings.
questions.trap: Picking 'hastens' without checking the sense.
wrongReasons: 'Hauls' means to pull or carry
'Halves' means to divide into two
'Hastens' means to speed up, the opposite of the meaning needed
steps: Spot what the question tests: Context clues in cloze.
Option A (hauls) is out: 'Hauls' means to pull or carry.
Option C (halves) is out: 'Halves' means to divide into two.
Option D (hastens) is out: 'Hastens' means to speed up, the opposite of the meaning needed.
Common slip to avoid: Picking 'hastens' without checking the sense.
So the answer is option B: halts.

questions.text: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (4) in the passage.
questions.explanation: Shoppers waiting in the rain would chat about the price of onions, so 'debating' fits the relaxed scene.
questions.trap: Choosing 'deciding', which sounds purposeful.
wrongReasons: One cannot 'decide' a market price while waiting out the rain
Nobody is defending the price of onions
'Deducting' a price makes no sense here
steps: Spot what the question tests: Verb choice by context.
Option A (deciding) is out: One cannot 'decide' a market price while waiting out the rain.
Option B (defending) is out: Nobody is defending the price of onions.
Option D (deducting) is out: 'Deducting' a price makes no sense here.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing 'deciding', which sounds purposeful.
So the answer is option C: debating.

questions.text: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (5) in the passage.
questions.explanation: 'Quiet satisfaction' points to a positive experience, so 'enjoyed a good day's trade' is the natural fit.
questions.trap: Choosing 'endured' because it also begins with E.
wrongReasons: 'Endured' suggests suffering, which clashes with 'quiet satisfaction'
'Emptied a good day's trade' is not meaningful
'Entered a trade' changes the sense completely
steps: Spot what the question tests: Tone-consistent word choice.
Option A (endured) is out: 'Endured' suggests suffering, which clashes with 'quiet satisfaction'.
Option B (emptied) is out: 'Emptied a good day's trade' is not meaningful.
Option C (entered) is out: 'Entered a trade' changes the sense completely.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing 'endured' because it also begins with E.
So the answer is option D: enjoyed.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the author's stance in the passage?
questions.explanation: The passage reports defenders, critics and a third reformist group, then closes by saying neither side has offered a convincing answer.
questions.trap: Taking the reporting of the critics' view as the author's own.
options: A balanced observer who finds neither side's case fully convincing
A supporter of reform who treats the critics' case as decisive
A defender of the present system who thinks the critics are mistaken
A sceptic who believes no reform can ever work
wrongReasons: The author says reforms face a central difficulty
Critics' points are reported without rebuttal
The author questions whether reforms can be introduced well, not whether they can ever work
steps: Spot what the question tests: Tone: balanced reporting vs advocacy.
Option B (A supporter of reform who treats the critics' c…) is out: The author says reforms face a central difficulty.
Option C (A defender of the present system who thinks the…) is out: Critics' points are reported without rebuttal.
Option D (A sceptic who believes no reform can ever work) is out: The author questions whether reforms can be introduced well, not whether they can ever work.
Common slip to avoid: Taking the reporting of the critics' view as the author's own.
So the answer is option A: A balanced observer who finds neither side's case fully convincing.

questions.text: According to the passage, critics of examinations argue all of the following EXCEPT that:
questions.explanation: Favouritism by examiners is what defenders say examinations curb; critics are never reported as alleging it.
questions.trap: Picking a stated point when the question asks for the one NOT stated.
questions.revise: EXCEPT questions: verify each option against the text
options: recall-based papers favour students who can afford coaching
gifts such as judgement and collaboration go unrewarded
examiners mark candidates they personally know more generously
the contest is unequal in a well-disguised way
wrongReasons: Stated: examinations reward recall and rehearsal
Stated: such gifts are penalised
Stated: an advantage for the already prepared
steps: Spot what the question tests: EXCEPT questions: verify each option against the text.
Option A (recall-based papers favour students who can aff…) is out: Stated: examinations reward recall and rehearsal.
Option B (gifts such as judgement and collaboration go un…) is out: Stated: such gifts are penalised.
Option D (the contest is unequal in a well-disguised way) is out: Stated: an advantage for the already prepared.
Common slip to avoid: Picking a stated point when the question asks for the one NOT stated.
So the answer is option C: examiners mark candidates they personally know more generously.

questions.text: The word 'pragmatic' as used in the passage most nearly means:
questions.explanation: The third group weighs what would actually happen if examinations were abolished, so 'pragmatic' means practical.
questions.trap: Reading 'pragmatic' as 'negative'.
options: concerned with practical results rather than ideals
wrongReasons: The third group favours reform, so it is not pessimistic
The group is worried about hidden unfairness
The group proposes reforms, not preservation
steps: Spot what the question tests: Vocabulary in context: pragmatic.
Option B (pessimistic about any change) is out: The third group favours reform, so it is not pessimistic.
Option C (indifferent to fairness) is out: The group is worried about hidden unfairness.
Option D (guided by tradition) is out: The group proposes reforms, not preservation.
Common slip to avoid: Reading 'pragmatic' as 'negative'.
So the answer is option A: concerned with practical results rather than ideals.

questions.text: It can be inferred from the passage that the third group would be LEAST likely to support:
questions.explanation: They say interviews would bring hidden inequality, since personal contacts count for even more.
questions.trap: Choosing a reform they themselves propose.
options: publishing the weightage of each topic in advance
wrongReasons: They propose this reform
They propose this reform
They propose this reform
steps: Spot what the question tests: Inference: what the group rejects.
Options A, B and C are out: They propose this reform.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing a reform they themselves propose.
So the answer is option D: replacing examinations with interviews.

questions.text: Why does the author mention interviews in the last paragraph?
questions.explanation: Interviews are given as the example of a hidden inequality that would replace the visible one.
questions.trap: Reversing the direction of the example.
options: To argue that interviews measure ability better than examinations
To suggest that coaching cannot help in interviews
To show that scrapping examinations could replace a visible unfairness with a concealed one
To claim that personal contacts matter less than critics allege
wrongReasons: The author says personal contacts count more in interviews
Not discussed in the passage
The passage says they matter even more
steps: Spot what the question tests: Purpose of an example.
Option A (To argue that interviews measure ability better…) is out: The author says personal contacts count more in interviews.
Option B (To suggest that coaching cannot help in intervi…) is out: Not discussed in the passage.
Option D (To claim that personal contacts matter less tha…) is out: The passage says they matter even more.
Common slip to avoid: Reversing the direction of the example.
So the answer is option C: To show that scrapping examinations could replace a visible unfairnes….

questions.text: Which of the following best expresses the main argument of the passage?
questions.explanation: The author argues that lending figures are an outdated measure and that libraries matter for who would be left behind without them.
questions.trap: Choosing a statement that is true of the passage's background but not its argument.
options: Libraries are declining because readers prefer screens, so councils are right to cut them
Libraries deserve support for the space and services they offer to people who would otherwise be left out, not for the books they lend
Borrowing figures show that libraries remain as popular as ever
Online access has made library buildings unnecessary but books still matter
wrongReasons: The author rejects the reasoning of those councils
The passage says borrowing has been falling
The author says online access is itself unequal
steps: Spot what the question tests: Main idea vs supporting detail.
Option A (Libraries are declining because readers prefer…) is out: The author rejects the reasoning of those councils.
Option C (Borrowing figures show that libraries remain as…) is out: The passage says borrowing has been falling.
Option D (Online access has made library buildings unnece…) is out: The author says online access is itself unequal.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing a statement that is true of the passage's background but not its argument.
So the answer is option B: Libraries deserve support for the space and services they offer to pe….

questions.text: According to the passage, councils that cut library services have overlooked the fact that:
questions.explanation: The passage says internet access is itself unequal, so those who most need a library are often without good connections at home.
questions.trap: Choosing a plausible claim that the passage never makes.
options: borrowing has risen in recent years
the people who most need a free, staffed space often lack good internet access at home
paper books are cheaper than online resources
librarians prefer a staffed space to a digital one
wrongReasons: The passage says borrowing has been falling
Not stated
Not stated; the point is about users' needs
steps: Spot what the question tests: Retrieval: stay with the text.
Option A (borrowing has risen in recent years) is out: The passage says borrowing has been falling.
Option C (paper books are cheaper than online resources) is out: Not stated.
Option D (librarians prefer a staffed space to a digital…) is out: Not stated; the point is about users' needs.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing a plausible claim that the passage never makes.
So the answer is option B: the people who most need a free, staffed space often lack good intern….

questions.text: The phrase 'a plain calculation' in the last sentence suggests that the author regards the case for libraries as:
questions.explanation: 'Plain' means simple and clear, and the sentence contrasts it with nostalgia for paper.
questions.trap: Missing the contrast with nostalgia.
options: a matter of straightforward reasoning about who would be disadvantaged
a legal argument based on council duties
wrongReasons: The author explicitly says it is not nostalgia
'Plain' means simple, not complicated
Not mentioned
steps: Spot what the question tests: Contrast signals in a sentence.
Option B (an emotional appeal to nostalgia) is out: The author explicitly says it is not nostalgia.
Option C (a complicated economic model) is out: 'Plain' means simple, not complicated.
Option D (a legal argument based on council duties) is out: Not mentioned.
Common slip to avoid: Missing the contrast with nostalgia.
So the answer is option A: a matter of straightforward reasoning about who would be disadvantaged.

questions.text: All of the following are mentioned as things a modern library offers EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The passage lists study space, job applications, software learning and company, but never e-book lending.
questions.trap: Not checking each option against the text.
options: a place to study without paying
access to e-books that can be borrowed from home
the chance to learn unfamiliar software
wrongReasons: Stated
Stated
Stated
steps: Spot what the question tests: EXCEPT questions.
Options A, C and D are out: Stated.
Common slip to avoid: Not checking each option against the text.
So the answer is option B: access to e-books that can be borrowed from home.

questions.text: The author would most likely agree that closing a library branch to save money:
questions.explanation: The passage says a closure may save money on paper but cost the community far more in lost opportunity.
questions.trap: Picking an option that sounds sensible but is not the author's view.
options: is justified whenever borrowing figures fall
may cost the community more than it saves
is acceptable if a free online alternative exists
should be combined with larger spending on paper books
wrongReasons: The author calls borrowing an outdated measure
Online access is described as unequal
The author's case is not about paper
steps: Spot what the question tests: Author's view vs general sense.
Option A (is justified whenever borrowing figures fall) is out: The author calls borrowing an outdated measure.
Option C (is acceptable if a free online alternative exis…) is out: Online access is described as unequal.
Option D (should be combined with larger spending on pape…) is out: The author's case is not about paper.
Common slip to avoid: Picking an option that sounds sensible but is not the author's view.
So the answer is option B: may cost the community more than it saves.

questions.text: Which of the following is supported by the passage?
questions.explanation: The experiments reported found a sleep advantage even when waking volunteers were allowed to rest.
questions.trap: Choosing an option that reverses a detail.
options: Rest while awake improves memory as much as sleep does
Sleep helps only with remembering simple facts
Volunteers who slept after learning did better the next morning than those who stayed awake, even when the waking group rested
The sleeping brain can learn new material on its own
wrongReasons: The waking group had time to rest and still did worse
The passage says the benefit is not confined to simple facts
The passage says a student who learnt nothing has nothing to consolidate
steps: Spot what the question tests: Retrieval: reversed details.
Option A (Rest while awake improves memory as much as sle…) is out: The waking group had time to rest and still did worse.
Option B (Sleep helps only with remembering simple facts) is out: The passage says the benefit is not confined to simple facts.
Option D (The sleeping brain can learn new material on it…) is out: The passage says a student who learnt nothing has nothing to consolidate.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing an option that reverses a detail.
So the answer is option C: Volunteers who slept after learning did better the next morning than….

questions.text: The author mentions a problem that 'seemed hopeless at midnight' in order to:
questions.explanation: The example is offered right after the claim that sleep helps people notice patterns.
questions.trap: Missing why an example appears where it does.
options: illustrate that sleep may help people notice patterns they had missed
show that people should avoid working at night
prove that problems become easier with time alone
suggest that the brain switches off during sleep
wrongReasons: Not claimed
The claim concerns sleep
The passage rejects this view
steps: Spot what the question tests: Purpose of an example.
Option B (show that people should avoid working at night) is out: Not claimed.
Option C (prove that problems become easier with time alo…) is out: The claim concerns sleep.
Option D (suggest that the brain switches off during sleep) is out: The passage rejects this view.
Common slip to avoid: Missing why an example appears where it does.
So the answer is option A: illustrate that sleep may help people notice patterns they had missed.

questions.text: The word 'consolidate' as used in the passage most nearly means:
questions.explanation: The sleeping brain strengthens memories, so 'consolidate' means to make firmer.
questions.trap: Choosing the dictionary's commonest sense.
wrongReasons: A common meaning, but not the sense here
The brain 'discards' some memories, but consolidation is about keeping
No speech is involved
steps: Spot what the question tests: Vocabulary in context: consolidate.
Option A (combine into a single unit) is out: A common meaning, but not the sense here.
Option C (erase gradually) is out: The brain 'discards' some memories, but consolidation is about keeping.
Option D (revise aloud) is out: No speech is involved.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing the dictionary's commonest sense.
So the answer is option B: make firmer and more secure.

questions.text: When the author says sleep 'cannot substitute for study', the implication is that:
questions.explanation: A student who has learnt nothing has nothing for the sleeping brain to consolidate.
questions.trap: Over-reading 'cannot substitute' as 'is useless'.
options: sleep is of no help in learning
study and sleep are equally important
sleep strengthens only what has already been learned
studying late at night is harmful
wrongReasons: The passage says sleep helps learning
Not claimed; sleep consolidates what study provides
Not stated; cramming is criticised for costing sleep
steps: Spot what the question tests: Inference: scope of a claim.
Option A (sleep is of no help in learning) is out: The passage says sleep helps learning.
Option B (study and sleep are equally important) is out: Not claimed; sleep consolidates what study provides.
Option D (studying late at night is harmful) is out: Not stated; cramming is criticised for costing sleep.
Common slip to avoid: Over-reading 'cannot substitute' as 'is useless'.
So the answer is option C: sleep strengthens only what has already been learned.

questions.text: Which of the following best captures the author's recommendation?
questions.explanation: The last sentence says the sensible approach is to treat sleep as part of preparation.
questions.trap: Picking an extreme version of the advice.
options: Treat sleep as part of preparation rather than as a rival to it
Sleep immediately before an examination to improve recall
wrongReasons: The passage does not suggest reducing study
Cramming is described as self-defeating
The point is about preparation, not the last hour
steps: Spot what the question tests: Concluding recommendation.
Option B (Study less and sleep more) is out: The passage does not suggest reducing study.
Option C (Cram only when well rested) is out: Cramming is described as self-defeating.
Option D (Sleep immediately before an examination to impr…) is out: The point is about preparation, not the last hour.
Common slip to avoid: Picking an extreme version of the advice.
So the answer is option A: Treat sleep as part of preparation rather than as a rival to it.

questions.text:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error.
A number of students / is waiting / outside the office / for the results.
questions.explanation: 'A number of' means 'several' and takes a plural verb: 'are waiting'. ('The number of' would take a singular verb.)
questions.trap: Matching the verb to the singular word 'number'.
wrongReasons: Subject phrase is correct
Prepositional phrase is correct
Phrase is correct
steps: Spot what the question tests: 'A number of' versus 'The number of'.
Option A (A number of students) is out: Subject phrase is correct.
Option B (outside the office) is out: Prepositional phrase is correct.
Option C (for the results) is out: Phrase is correct.
Common slip to avoid: Matching the verb to the singular word 'number'.
So the answer is option D: is waiting.

questions.text:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error.
This is the most unique / design that / the architect has / ever produced.
questions.explanation: 'Unique' means one of a kind, so it cannot be compared with 'most'. The correct phrase is 'the most distinctive' or simply 'unique'.
questions.trap: Accepting 'most unique' because it is common in speech.
wrongReasons: Phrase is correct
Phrase is correct
Phrase is correct
steps: Spot what the question tests: Absolute adjectives (unique, perfect, complete).
Options A, C and D are out: Phrase is correct.
Common slip to avoid: Accepting 'most unique' because it is common in speech.
So the answer is option B: This is the most unique.

questions.text:
Select the option that improves the underlined part of the sentence. If no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement'.
Had I known about the traffic, I __will have left__ earlier.
questions.explanation: 'Had I known' is an inverted third conditional, so the main clause takes 'would have + past participle'.
questions.trap: Choosing 'will have' because the sentence feels like future perfect.
wrongReasons: 'Will have left' does not fit a past unreal condition
The main clause needs 'would have'
This expresses a present or future result
steps: Spot what the question tests: Inverted third conditional.
Option A (No improvement) is out: 'Will have left' does not fit a past unreal condition.
Option B (had left) is out: The main clause needs 'would have'.
Option C (would leave) is out: This expresses a present or future result.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing 'will have' because the sentence feels like future perfect.
So the answer is option D: would have left.

questions.text:
Select the option that improves the underlined part of the sentence. If no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement'.
He asked me where __was I going__.
questions.explanation: In an embedded question the word order is subject + verb: 'where I was going'.
questions.trap: Keeping the inverted order of a direct question.
wrongReasons: An indirect question keeps statement word order
Retains question order and adds 'to'
Changes both order and tense
steps: Spot what the question tests: Word order in indirect questions.
Option A (No improvement) is out: An indirect question keeps statement word order.
Option B (was I going to) is out: Retains question order and adds 'to'.
Option C (did I go) is out: Changes both order and tense.
Common slip to avoid: Keeping the inverted order of a direct question.
So the answer is option D: I was going.

questions.text:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate word.
She was so ______ in her work that she did not notice the visitors arrive.
questions.explanation: 'Absorbed in' means deeply engrossed. 'Absorbing' would describe the work, not the person.
questions.trap: Confusing -ed and -ing adjectives.
wrongReasons: The participle means 'interesting', not 'engrossed'
A noun does not fit after 'was so'
'Absorbent' describes materials that soak up liquid
steps: Spot what the question tests: Participial adjectives: -ed versus -ing.
Option B (absorbing) is out: The participle means 'interesting', not 'engrossed'.
Option C (absorption) is out: A noun does not fit after 'was so'.
Option D (absorbent) is out: 'Absorbent' describes materials that soak up liquid.
Common slip to avoid: Confusing -ed and -ing adjectives.
So the answer is option A: absorbed.

questions.text:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate word.
The discovery of the manuscript has shed new light ______ the poet's early life.
questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is 'shed light on', meaning to clarify.
questions.trap: Choosing 'over' from the sense of covering.
wrongReasons: 'Shed light at' is not used
'Over' does not fit this idiom
'Shed light with' is not used
steps: Spot what the question tests: Fixed prepositions with idioms.
Option B (at) is out: 'Shed light at' is not used.
Option C (over) is out: 'Over' does not fit this idiom.
Option D (with) is out: 'Shed light with' is not used.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing 'over' from the sense of covering.
So the answer is option A: on.

questions.text: Choose the word closest in meaning to: ABSTRUSE
questions.explanation: 'Abstruse' means difficult to understand; 'obscure' is the closest.
questions.trap: Picking 'absurd' because of the similar sound.
wrongReasons: Opposite in sense
Sounds similar but means ridiculous
Sounds similar but means sudden
steps: Spot what the question tests: Look-alike words.
Option A (obvious) is out: Opposite in sense.
Option B (absurd) is out: Sounds similar but means ridiculous.
Option D (abrupt) is out: Sounds similar but means sudden.
Common slip to avoid: Picking 'absurd' because of the similar sound.
So the answer is option C: obscure.

questions.text: Choose the word opposite in meaning to: EXPEDITE
questions.explanation: 'Expedite' means to speed up a process; 'delay' is the opposite.
questions.trap: Choosing 'hasten', a synonym.
wrongReasons: A synonym of 'expedite'
A synonym of 'expedite'
Unrelated to speed
steps: Spot what the question tests: Words of speed and delay.
Options A and B are out: A synonym of 'expedite'.
Option D (execute) is out: Unrelated to speed.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing 'hasten', a synonym.
So the answer is option C: delay.

questions.text: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: To bite the bullet
questions.explanation: 'Bite the bullet' means to endure a painful or difficult situation with courage.
questions.trap: Interpreting it literally.
options: To face an unpleasant situation bravely
wrongReasons: Literal misreading
Not the meaning
Opposite of confronting a problem
steps: Spot what the question tests: Common idioms with 'bite'.
Option A (To eat hurriedly) is out: Literal misreading.
Option C (To speak harshly) is out: Not the meaning.
Option D (To avoid a quarrel) is out: Opposite of confronting a problem.
Common slip to avoid: Interpreting it literally.
So the answer is option B: To face an unpleasant situation bravely.

questions.text: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: To add insult to injury
questions.explanation: The idiom means to worsen a bad situation by further offence.
questions.trap: Taking 'injury' literally.
options: To make a bad situation worse
wrongReasons: Opposite in effect
Literal misreading
Not the meaning
steps: Spot what the question tests: Idioms about misfortune.
Option A (To apologise after a quarrel) is out: Opposite in effect.
Option B (To treat a wound) is out: Literal misreading.
Option C (To complain loudly) is out: Not the meaning.

questions.text:
Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful sentence or paragraph.
P. However, it is rarely talent alone that decides the outcome.
Q. Every field has its prodigies, people who seem to master a skill almost effortlessly.
R. Steady practice, repeated over years, usually separates the accomplished from the merely gifted.
S. Observers often attribute their success to natural ability.
questions.explanation: Q introduces prodigies; S ('their success') follows; P ('However') contrasts that view; R completes the argument.
questions.trap: Starting with S, which refers back to something unnamed.
questions.revise: Pronoun and connector clues in jumbles
wrongReasons: 'Their success' needs the prodigies of Q first
'However' cannot come before the claim it contradicts
Opens with a connector that has nothing to contrast
steps: Spot what the question tests: Pronoun and connector clues in jumbles.
Option A (SQPR) is out: 'Their success' needs the prodigies of Q first.
Option C (QPSR) is out: 'However' cannot come before the claim it contradicts.
Option D (PQRS) is out: Opens with a connector that has nothing to contrast.
Common slip to avoid: Starting with S, which refers back to something unnamed.
So the answer is option B: QSPR.

questions.text:

A relative clause cannot open the sentence
The reason clause cannot precede the verb

Option C (SRQP) is out: A relative clause cannot open the sentence.
Option D (RSPQ) is out: The reason clause cannot precede the verb.
Common slip to avoid: Putting the main verb before the relative clause.
So the answer is option A: RSQP.

questions.text:

questions.trap: Placing P right after Q and skipping the cause.
wrongReasons: 'As a result' needs the cause (S) before it
'This fall' in S needs Q to come first
'Such a shift' in R needs P before it
steps: Spot what the question tests: Cause-effect order in jumbles.
Option A (QPSR) is out: 'As a result' needs the cause (S) before it.
Option B (SQPR) is out: 'This fall' in S needs Q to come first.
Option C (QSRP) is out: 'Such a shift' in R needs P before it.
Common slip to avoid: Placing P right after Q and skipping the cause.
So the answer is option D: QSPR.

questions.text:

questions.text:
